pages.x: In 1855 Mexico's liberals came to power and began to strip the Catholic Church and the army of their old privileges: their own law courts and, for the Church, its vast lands. The new constitution of 1857 made all citizens equal before the law. The bishops threatened to excommunicate anyone who swore to uphold it, and conservatives got ready to fight.

In December 1857 the moderate president, Ignacio Comonfort, joined a conservative coup, the Plan of Tacubaya, and shut down Congress. Within weeks he had lost control, and conservative generals took the capital. Benito Juárez, head of the Supreme Court and by law next in line, declared himself president and set up a liberal government outside the city.

Juárez was a Zapotec from a poor village in Oaxaca, orphaned young, who had worked his way through school to become a lawyer. In Guadalajara in March 1858 mutinous soldiers seized him and raised their rifles to shoot him. The poet Guillermo Prieto stepped in front of him and cried out that the brave do not murder, and the soldiers lowered their guns.

Juárez escaped to the Pacific and sailed by way of Panama, Havana and New Orleans to Veracruz, which he reached in May 1858. Behind its walls, paid by the duties on its trade, his government held out for three years. In the centre of the country the conservatives, led by the brilliant young general Miguel Miramón, won battle after battle.

In April 1859 a liberal army attacked Mexico City and was beaten at Tacubaya by the conservative general Leonardo Márquez. He had the prisoners shot, and with them the doctors and medical students who had stayed to care for the wounded of both sides. Mexicans called him the Tiger of Tacubaya.

From Veracruz in 1859 Juárez struck back with the Reform Laws. The state took over the property of the Church, made marriage a civil contract, kept the records of births and deaths, and ran the cemeteries.
pages.fx: In 1860 came freedom of religion. Church and state in Mexico were separated, as they still are, and sales of Church land helped pay for the war.

pages.x: In March 1860 Miramón besieged Veracruz again, with two small warships bought in Havana to blockade it from the sea. Juárez called them pirates, and a United States Navy squadron, friendly to the liberals, seized them off Antón Lizardo. Without them the siege failed, and the war began to turn.

Liberal armies from the north and west closed in. On 22 December 1860, at Calpulalpan, Jesús González Ortega crushed Miramón's last army. Miramón fled abroad, liberal troops marched into Mexico City, and in January 1861 Juárez came back to the capital he had left three years before.

The war left Mexico ruined. In 1861 Juárez stopped paying its foreign debts for two years, and France, Spain and Britain sent troops to collect. Napoleon III used the chance to put an emperor on the throne of Mexico, and the liberals had to fight again until 1867. But the Reform's separation of Church and state lasts.
